3cp class=\"note-text-block\">“If unstable, synchronized cardioversion. If stable, rate control, anticoagulation according to\u003cbr>stroke risk, treat triggers, and avoid verapamil/diltiazem in HFrEF.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ward-round summary\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“Management of heart failure starts by classifying the patient by EF, NYHA class, ACC/AHA\u003cbr>stage, and congestion/perfusion profile. In acute decompensated HF, I start with ABCDE,\u003cbr>oxygen only if hypoxic, NIV/CPAP if pulmonary edema with distress, ECG, CXR, renal\u003cbr>function, electrolytes, troponin if ACS suspected, and echocardiography. If warm-wet, give IV\u003cbr>furosemide 40–80 mg and monitor urine output, weight, BP, renal function and electrolytes. If\u003cbr>hypertensive pulmonary edema, add nitrates if SBP allows. If cold-wet/cardiogenic shock, admit\u003cbr>ICU, give noradrenaline for perfusion pressure and dobutamine for contractility, avoid blind\u003cbr>fluids, and cautiously decongest after perfusion is supported. Long-term HFrEF therapy uses four\u003cbr>pillars: ARNI/ACEi/ARB, evidence-based beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor, plus\u003cbr>diuretics for congestion and treatment of triggers.”\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 24\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">HEART FAILURE — MASTER FRAMEWORK\u003c/h3>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Definition\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the\u003cbr>metabolic demands of the body, or can do so only at the expense of raised filling pressures.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In simple ward language:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Heart failure = symptoms/signs of congestion or low cardiac output due to structural or\u003cbr>functional cardiac abnormality.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It is not diagnosed by one symptom alone. You must combine:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  history,   •  examination,   •  CXR/ECG,   •  BNP/NT-proBNP if available,   •  echocardiography.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">AHA/ACC/HFSA defines HF as a complex clinical syndrome with symptoms and signs caused\u003cbr>by structural or functional cardiac abnormality, supported by elevated natriuretic peptides or\u003cbr>objective evidence of congestion.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Classification of Heart Failure\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A. By ejection fraction\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Type\u003c/td>\u003ctd>EF\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Meaning\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>HFrEF\u003c/td>\u003ctd>≤40%\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>HFmrEF\u003c/td>\u003ctd>41–49%\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Heart failure with mildly reduced EF\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>HFpEF\u003c/td>\u003ctd>≥50%\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Heart failure with preserved EF\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>HFimpEF\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Previously ≤40%, now &gt;40%\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Improved EF after treatment\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This matters because HFrEF has strongest evidence for four-pillar therapy.\u003cbr>AHA/ACC/HFSA states guideline-directed medical therapy for HFrEF includes four major\u003cbr>medication classes, including SGLT2 inhibitors.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">B. By ACC/AHA stages\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Stage\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Meaning\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Example\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>A\u003c/td>\u003ctd>At risk, no structural\u003cbr>disease/symptoms\u003c/td>\u003ctd>HTN, DM, obesity\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 25\u003c/div>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>B\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Structural heart disease, no\u003cbr>symptoms\u003c/td>\u003ctd>LVH, low EF but asymptomatic\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>C\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Structural disease with symptoms\u003c/td>\u003ctd>dyspnea, edema, orthopnea\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>D\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Advanced HF\u003c/td>\u003ctd>recurrent admissions, inotrope dependence,\u003cbr>refractory symptoms\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Advanced HF is usually Stage D. The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline describes HF stages as\u003cbr>a continuum from at-risk to advanced disease.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">C. By NYHA functional class\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>NYHA\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Functional limitation\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>I\u003c/td>\u003ctd>No limitation\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>II\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Symptoms with ordinary activity\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>III\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Symptoms with less-than-ordinary activity\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>IV\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Symptoms at rest\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Panel likes this. If your diagnosis is heart failure, say:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“Congestive heart failure NYHA class IV secondary to hypertensive heart disease.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Not just “heart failure.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">D. By congestion and perfusion\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is very useful in acute ward management.\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Profile\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Meaning\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Treatment direction\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Warm and\u003cbr>wet\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Perfused but congested\u003c/td>\u003ctd>IV diuretics ± nitrates\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Cold and wet\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Hypoperfused and\u003cbr>congested\u003c/td>\u003ctd>ICU, noradrenaline/dobutamine, cautious\u003cbr>diuresis\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Cold and dry\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Hypoperfused and\u003cbr>underfilled\u003c/td>\u003ctd>small fluid challenge ± inotrope\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Warm and\u003cbr>dry\u003c/td>\u003ctd>compensated\u003c/td>\u003ctd>optimize chronic therapy\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">For exams, always ask:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Is the patient congested? Is the patient perfused?\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Causes of Heart Failure\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A. Common causes in Tanzania/KCMC setting\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 26\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. Hypertensive heart disease\u003cbr>2. Rheumatic heart disease\u003cbr>3. Dilated cardiomyopathy\u003cbr>4. Ischemic heart disease\u003cbr>5. Alcohol-related cardiomyopathy\u003cbr>6. Peripartum cardiomyopathy\u003cbr>7. Myocarditis\u003cbr>8. HIV-related cardiomyopathy\u003cbr>9. Thyroid disease\u003cbr>10. Anemia\u003cbr>11. Chronic kidney disease\u003cbr>12. Cor pulmonale from COPD/PTB/ILD\u003cbr>13. Constrictive pericarditis, especially TB-related\u003cbr>14. Valvular heart disease\u003cbr>15. Arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">B. Causes of dilated cardiomyopathy\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If panel asks “other causes apart from alcohol,” say:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>idiopathic,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>genetic/familial,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>viral myocarditis,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>HIV,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>peripartum cardiomyopathy,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>chemotherapy, for example doxorubicin,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>thyroid disease,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>nutritional deficiency, for example thiamine,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>autoimmune disease,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>ischemic cardiomyopathy,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>chronic uncontrolled hypertension,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>toxins.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. Precipitating factors for acute decompensation\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Use FAILURE.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Letter\u003cbr>Cause\u003cbr>F\u003cbr>Forgotten drugs / poor adherence\u003cbr>A\u003cbr>Arrhythmia, especially AF\u003cbr>I\u003cbr>Ischemia or infection\u003cbr>L\u003cbr>Lifestyle: salt/fluid excess, alcohol, NSAIDs\u003cbr>U\u003cbr>Uncontrolled hypertension\u003cbr>R\u003cbr>Renal failure, pulmonary embolism\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 27\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Letter  Cause  E  Endocrine/anemia: thyroid disease, severe anemia\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is high yield because many questions come from: “Why did this patient decompensate?”\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">5. History Taking in Heart Failure\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A. Dyspnea amplification\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Do not just write “difficulty in breathing.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ask:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>onset,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>duration,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>progression,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>exertional or at rest,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>how far can patient walk now?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>what could they do before?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>can they climb stairs?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>can they bathe/dress/feed themselves?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>orthopnea: how many pillows and for how long?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>PND: wakes from sleep gasping?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>cough: dry/frothy/pink sputum?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>wheeze: cardiac asthma or COPD?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>chest pain,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>palpitations,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>syncope.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Panel asked: “Amplification ya dyspnea: what can the patient do currently and what can’t  she do?”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">That is how you assign NYHA.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">B. Orthopnea\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If you write “uses more than 2 pillows,” be ready to answer:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>since when?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>previously how many pillows?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>now how many?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>does breathlessness improve when sitting?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>can the patient lie flat?\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 28\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Orthopnea indicates raised left-sided filling pressure/pulmonary congestion.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">C. Edema\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ask:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>onset,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>starts at ankles?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>bilateral or unilateral?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pitting or non-pitting?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>progression to thighs/abdomen?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>worse evening?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>associated abdominal distension?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>facial puffiness?\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>reduced urine?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In examination, report:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“Bilateral pitting lower limb edema up to mid-shin/knee, grade 2.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">D. Risk factors and cause\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ask for:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>hypertension duration/control/drugs/adherence,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>diabetes,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>alcohol,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>smoking,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>previous rheumatic fever,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>sore throat history,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>known valvular disease,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>chest pain/MI,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>HIV,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>chemotherapy,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pregnancy/postpartum,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>thyroid symptoms,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>TB/pericarditis history,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>renal disease,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>family history of cardiomyopathy/sudden death.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 29\u003c/div>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">6. Physical Examination\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A. General examination\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Look for:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>respiratory distress,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>orthopneic posture,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pallor,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>cyanosis,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>jaundice,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>clubbing,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>edema,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>cachexia,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>raised JVP,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>thyroid signs,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pulse rate/rhythm/volume,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>BP.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If patient is pale, include anemia in diagnosis.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Example:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“Acute decompensated heart failure NYHA IV secondary to hypertensive heart disease,  complicated by severe anemia.”\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">B. Pulse\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Assess:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>rate,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>rhythm,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>volume,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>character,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>radio-radial delay,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>radio-femoral delay,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>collapsing pulse.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">AF on physical exam:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  irregularly irregular pulse,   •  variable pulse volume,   •  pulse deficit between apex and radial pulse.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">C. JVP assessment\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 30\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Panel loves JVP.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">How to assess JVP\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. Position patient at 45 degrees.\u003cbr>2. Turn head slightly to the left.\u003cbr>3. Use tangential light.\u003cbr>4. Identify venous pulsation between two heads of sternocleidomastoid.\u003cbr>5. Measure vertical height above sternal angle.\u003cbr>6. Normal JVP is usually ≤3–4 cm above sternal angle.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Which vein?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mainly the right internal jugular vein.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Anatomical location\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">The internal jugular vein lies deep to sternocleidomastoid, between its sternal and clavicular\u003cbr>heads, draining into the brachiocephalic vein.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">JVP vs carotid\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>JVP\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Carotid\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>non-palpable\u003c/td>\u003ctd>palpable\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>biphasic waveform\u003c/td>\u003ctd>single upstroke\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>varies with respiration\u003c/td>\u003ctd>does not vary much\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>changes with position\u003c/td>\u003ctd>little change\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>obliterated by gentle pressure\u003c/td>\u003ctd>not obliterated\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>rises with hepatojugular reflux\u003c/td>\u003ctd>no such rise\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">D. Hepatojugular reflux\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">How to do:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. Patient at 45 degrees.\u003cbr>2. Observe baseline JVP.\u003cbr>3. Apply firm pressure over right upper abdomen/liver for 10–30 seconds.\u003cbr>4. Positive if JVP rises and remains elevated during pressure.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Meaning:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  elevated right-sided filling pressure,   •  RV failure,\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 31\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  fluid overload,   •  constrictive pericarditis,   •  severe TR.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">E. Apex beat\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Panel asked this repeatedly.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Report:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>visible or not,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>palpable or not,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>location: intercostal space and relation to midclavicular line,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>character: tapping/heaving/thrusting,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>displaced or not.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Example:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“Apex beat is displaced to the 6th intercostal space anterior axillary line, diffuse and\u003cbr>thrusting, suggesting LV dilatation.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Do not just say: “6th intercostal space.” Say whether it is displaced.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">F. Murmurs\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If you hear a pansystolic murmur, know differentials:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable in expiration/left\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>lateral\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>TR\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>lower left sternal\u003cbr>edge\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>right lower\u003cbr>sternal/epigastrium\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>louder on inspiration\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>VSD\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>left lower sternal\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>widespread\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>harsh, thrill possible\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>edge\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">How DCM causes MR\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">DCM causes LV dilatation → mitral annular dilatation → papillary muscle displacement →\u003cbr>failure of leaflet coaptation → functional mitral regurgitation.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">G. Respiratory system\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Do not forget:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  respiratory rate,   •  chest expansion,\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 32\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  percussion,   •  breath sounds,   •  added sounds,   •  vocal resonance.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Panel specifically noted students forgot vocal resonance.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Findings in HF:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  bibasal crackles,   •  pleural effusion signs,   •  wheeze/cardiac asthma.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">H. Abdomen\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Assess:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>hepatomegaly,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>ascites,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>splenomegaly,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>tenderness,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>liver span,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>shifting dullness,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>fluid thrill.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hepatomegaly measurement\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Measure from right costal margin in midclavicular line to the lower liver edge during inspiration.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Liver span\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Percuss upper and lower borders of liver in the right midclavicular line. Normal liver span is\u003cbr>roughly 6–12 cm in adults, depending body size.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">7. Diagnostic Criteria: Framingham Criteria\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Heart failure can be clinically diagnosed using Framingham criteria: 2 major criteria or 1  major + 2 minor criteria.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Major criteria\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  PND   •  Orthopnea   •  Raised JVP   •  Pulmonary crackles   •  S3 gallop\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 33\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Cardiomegaly on CXR\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Pulmonary edema on CXR\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Acute pulmonary edema\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Hepatojugular reflux\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Weight loss &gt;4.5 kg in 5 days in response to treatment\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Minor criteria\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>bilateral ankle edema\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>nocturnal cough\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>dyspnea on ordinary exertion\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>hepatomegaly\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pleural effusion\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>tachycardia &gt;120 bpm\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>decreased vital capacity\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Minor criteria should only be counted if not explained by another disease, for example COPD.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">8. Investigations\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">A. Bedside\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  pulse oximetry,   •  BP,   •  RBG,   •  ECG,   •  urine output.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">B. Blood tests\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>FBP: anemia/infection\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Urea, creatinine, eGFR\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Sodium, potassium, bicarbonate\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>LFTs\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Albumin\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>TSH if young/unexplained HF or thyroid signs\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Lipid profile\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>HbA1c/RBG\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Troponin if ACS suspected\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>BNP/NT-proBNP if available\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>HIV if cardiomyopathy risk\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>HBsAg/HCV if DCM/liver disease/ascites context\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>CRP/cultures if infection suspected\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">C. ECG\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 34\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ECG may show:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>AF,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>LVH,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>ischemia/MI,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>bundle branch block,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>chamber enlargement,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>arrhythmias,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>low voltage if pericardial effusion,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>RV strain/cor pulmonale.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">D. Chest X-ray\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Heart failure CXR findings:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>cardiomegaly,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>upper lobe diversion,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Kerley B lines,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pulmonary edema,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pleural effusion,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>bat-wing opacities,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>enlarged pulmonary arteries if pulmonary hypertension.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">COPD/cor pulmonale CXR:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>hyperinflation,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>flattened diaphragm,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>narrow vertical heart,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>prominent pulmonary arteries,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>RV enlargement.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">E. Echocardiography\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Echo is the key test.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">It tells:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>EF,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>chamber size,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>LVH,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>global vs regional hypokinesia,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>valvular lesions,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>RV function,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pulmonary hypertension,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pericardial effusion,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>thrombus,\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 35\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  diastolic function.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Expected echo in hypertensive heart disease:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  LVH,   •  diastolic dysfunction,   •  LA enlargement,   •  preserved or reduced EF depending stage.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Expected echo in DCM:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  dilated LV,   •  reduced EF,   •  global hypokinesia,   •  functional MR/TR,   •  possible pulmonary hypertension.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">F. BNP / NT-proBNP\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">BNP/NT-proBNP support HF diagnosis, especially when dyspnea cause is unclear.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">They rise in HF but can also rise in:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  CKD,   •  PE,   •  pulmonary hypertension,   •  sepsis,   •  older age.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">They may be lower in obesity.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">9. Differential diagnosis of dyspnea in HF patient\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Always investigate differentials.\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable loss\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>CXR, GeneXpert, CT\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">TB/ILD  chronic cough, weight loss  CXR, GeneXpert, CT\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">10. Management of Acute Decompensated Heart Failure\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 1: ABCDE\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Airway\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Assess airway. If low GCS, exhaustion, severe pulmonary edema, aspiration risk →  ICU/anesthesia.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Breathing\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Sit upright.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Oxygen if hypoxic.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Target SpO₂ ≥92%, or 88–92% if COPD/CO₂ retainer.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>NIV/CPAP if severe pulmonary edema.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Circulation\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>IV access.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>ECG monitor.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>BP monitoring.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Foley catheter if severe.\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Assess perfusion and congestion.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Disability\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  GCS,   •  RBG,   •  hypoperfusion signs.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Exposure\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Look for trigger: infection, ACS, PE, non-adherence, anemia, renal failure.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 2: If congested and perfused\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Give:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Furosemide 40 mg IV stat\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If severe congestion/CKD/already on furosemide:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Furosemide 40–80 mg IV stat, then reassess.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 37\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Monitor:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>urine output,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>weight,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>BP,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>creatinine,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>potassium,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>sodium,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>symptoms,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>oxygen requirement.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Panel asked: “How do you assess decongestion after diuretics?”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Answer:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>reduced dyspnea/orthopnea,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>reduced crackles,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>reduced JVP,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>reduced edema,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>improved oxygenation,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>increased urine output,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>negative fluid balance,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>weight loss,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>improved hepatomegaly/ascites if present.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 3: If hypertensive pulmonary edema\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If SBP &gt;110 and pulmonary edema:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  IV or sublingual nitrates if available,   •  furosemide,   •  NIV/CPAP.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Avoid nitrates in hypotension, severe AS, RV infarction, recent sildenafil.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 4: If cardiogenic shock / cold-wet\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Features:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>hypotension,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>cold extremities,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>confusion,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>oliguria,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>high lactate,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pulmonary edema/raised JVP.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 38\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Management:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>MICU/HDU,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>oxygen/NIV/intubation if needed,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>noradrenaline if hypotensive,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>dobutamine if poor contractility,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>cautious diuresis after perfusion support,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>urgent echo,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>treat cause.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hold:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  beta-blocker,   •  ACEi/ARB/ARNI,   •  spironolactone,   •  SGLT2 inhibitor,\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">if shock, AKI, hyperkalemia or severe hypotension.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">11. Chronic HFrEF Management — Four Pillars\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">For HFrEF EF ≤40%, use four pillars if tolerated:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. ARNI / ACEi / ARB\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Preferred internationally:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Sacubitril/valsartan\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Common local alternatives:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Enalapril 2.5–5 mg PO OD/BD, titrate   •  Losartan 25–50 mg PO OD, titrate\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Benefits:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  reduces mortality,   •  reduces hospitalization,   •  reduces remodeling.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Avoid/hold in:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  pregnancy,   •  hyperkalemia,   •  AKI,   •  bilateral renal artery stenosis,\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 39\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  severe hypotension.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Evidence-based beta blocker\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Use only when stable/euvolemic.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Options:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Carvedilol 3.125 mg PO BD, titrate   •  Bisoprolol 1.25 mg PO OD, titrate   •  Metoprolol succinate if available.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Benefits:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  reduces mortality,   •  reduces arrhythmia,   •  reduces remodeling.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Do not start/up-titrate in:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  acute pulmonary edema,   •  cardiogenic shock,   •  severe bradycardia,   •  severe hypotension.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Example:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Spironolactone 12.5–25 mg PO OD\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mechanism:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Blocks aldosterone receptor → reduces sodium/water retention, potassium excretion, fibrosis and  remodeling.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Side effects:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>hyperkalemia,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>gynecomastia,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>breast tenderness,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>menstrual irregularities,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>worsening renal function.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Alternative:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 40\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Eplerenone if available, less gynecomastia.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. SGLT2 inhibitor\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Options:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Dapagliflozin 10 mg PO OD   •  Empagliflozin 10 mg PO OD\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Benefits:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  reduces HF hospitalization,   •  renal protection,   •  works even without diabetes in HFrEF.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hold during:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  AKI,   •  shock,   •  severe dehydration,   •  DKA,   •  fasting/perioperative illness.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">ESC 2023 update strengthened SGLT2 inhibitor recommendations for HFmrEF/HFpEF, and\u003cbr>reviews summarize that dapagliflozin and empagliflozin received Class I Level A\u003cbr>recommendations in HFmrEF/HFpEF.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">12. HFpEF Management\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">For EF ≥50%:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>control BP,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>treat congestion with diuretics,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>manage AF,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>treat ischemia,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>manage obesity/DM/CKD/OSA,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>SGLT2 inhibitor if eligible,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>treat valvular disease.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">HFpEF is not “normal.” EF is preserved but filling pressure is high.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">13. Prognosis in Heart Failure\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Poor prognostic factors:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>NYHA IV,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>recurrent admissions,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>low EF,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>hyponatremia,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>CKD/cardiorenal syndrome,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>hypotension,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>high BNP/NT-proBNP,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pulmonary hypertension,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>RV dysfunction,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>severe MR/TR,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>cachexia,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>anemia,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>poor adherence,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>persistent congestion,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>inotrope requirement.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">15. Common Panel Questions and Model Answers\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Q1. How do you know patient has heart failure?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“By symptoms and signs of congestion or low output, supported by objective evidence. My\u003cbr>patient has dyspnea, orthopnea/PND, edema, raised JVP, basal crepitations, displaced apex, and\u003cbr>CXR/echo evidence. I would confirm with echocardiography and BNP/NT-proBNP if available.”\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 42\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Q2. Why classify NYHA?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“To grade functional limitation, severity and prognosis, and to monitor response to treatment.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Q3. What confirms HF?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“Echocardiography is the key test because it shows EF, chamber size, valves, wall motion, RV\u003cbr>function and pulmonary pressure. What do you monitor after furosemide?\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“Urine output, daily weight, BP, symptoms, edema, JVP, oxygenation, creatinine, sodium and  potassium.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Q5. define and classify the patient heart failure is a clinical syndrome where the heart fails to pump enough blood to meet body needs, or can do so only with raised filling pressures. it presents with dyspnea, orthopnea, pnd, fatigue, edema, raised jvp, pulmonary congestion, pleural effusion, ascites, or shock. before management, classify the patient properly: a. by ef type ef meaning hfref ≤40% heart failure with reduced ef hfmref 41–49% mildly reduced ef hfpef ≥50% preserved ef but raised filling pressures hfimpef previous ef ≤40%, now >40% improved ef after treatment this matters because hfref has the strongest mortality-reducing drug evidence. aha/acc/hfsa states that guideline-directed medical therapy for hfref includes four major drug classes. b. by nyha class nyha functional status i no limitation ii symptoms with ordinary activity iii symptoms with less-than-ordinary activity iv symptoms at rest always include nyha in diagnosis. example: “acute decompensated congestive heart failure nyha iv secondary to hypertensive heart disease.” c. by acc/aha stage stage meaning a at risk, no structural disease b structural heart disease, no symptoms c structural disease with current/past symptoms d advanced hf, refractory/recurrent symptoms d. by acute hemodynamic profile profile meaning management direction warm-wet perfused but congested iv diuretics ± nitrates cold-wet hypoperfused and congested icu, vasopressor/inotrope, cautious diuresis cold-dry hypoperfused but underfilled cautious fluid challenge ± inotrope warm-dry compensated optimize chronic therapy this is critical in ward rounds. do not give furosemide or fluids blindly. 2. general goals of management management aims to: 1. relieve congestion and dyspnea. 2. improve perfusion if shocked. 3. treat precipitating causes. 4. reduce mortality and hospitalization. 5. prevent progression/remodeling. 6. prevent complications: aki, arrhythmia, thromboembolism, electrolyte problems. 7. educate patient and prevent readmission. 3. initial management of acute decompensated heart failure step 1: abcde assessment a — airway assess whether the patient can protect airway. call icu/anesthesia early if: • reduced gcs, • severe respiratory distress, • exhaustion, • aspiration risk, • severe pulmonary edema not improving. b — breathing sit patient upright. give oxygen only if hypoxic. targets: • most patients: spo₂ ≥92% • copd/co₂ retainer: spo₂ 88–92% use cpap/niv if: • acute pulmonary edema, • severe respiratory distress, • hypoxia despite oxygen, • acidosis/hypercapnia, • patient conscious and cooperative. nice recommends considering niv without delay in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema with severe dyspnea and acidaemia or failure to respond to treatment. c — circulation do: • two iv lines, • ecg monitor, • bp/map monitoring, • check pulse rhythm, • assess jvp, • assess peripheral perfusion, • foley catheter if severe, • strict input/output chart. d — disability check: • gcs, • rbg, • confusion, • stroke signs, • hypoperfusion. e — exposure look for: • fever/infection, • anemia, • edema, • dvt, • ascites, • medication bottles, • nsaid/herbal use, • thyroid signs, • alcohol use. 4. investigations in acute hf do not delay emergency treatment, but investigate early. bedside • spo₂ • bp, pulse, rr, temperature • rbg • ecg • urine output blood tests • fbp • urea/creatinine/egfr • sodium, potassium, bicarbonate • magnesium • lfts/albumin • troponin if acs suspected • bnp/nt-probnp if diagnosis uncertain • crp/blood cultures if infection suspected • tsh if unexplained hf/af/thyroid features • hba1c/lipid profile after stabilization imaging • cxr • echocardiography • doppler/ctpa if pe suspected • renal ultrasound if aki/ckd or obstruction suspected echocardiography must answer • ef • lv size • global vs regional hypokinesia • rv function • pulmonary pressure • valves: mr, tr, as, ar, ms • pericardial effusion • thrombus • diastolic function 5. identify and treat precipitating factors use failure. letter trigger f forgotten drugs / poor adherence a arrhythmia, especially af i ischemia or infection l lifestyle: salt/fluid excess, alcohol, nsaids u uncontrolled hypertension r renal failure, pulmonary embolism e endocrine/anemia: thyroid disease, severe anemia in kcmc/tanzania, common triggers are poor adherence, uncontrolled hypertension, infection, anemia, renal failure, nsaids, excess salt/fluid, af, acs, pe, and late presentation. 6. management according to acute profile a. warm-wet heart failure this is the commonest admitted hf patient: congested but perfused. features: • dyspnea, • orthopnea, • raised jvp, • crackles, • edema, • ascites, • pleural effusion, • bp acceptable, • warm peripheries. treatment give iv loop diuretic. kcmc/tanzania practical regimen: • furosemide 40 mg iv stat if diuretic-naïve or mild-moderate congestion. • furosemide 40–80 mg iv stat if severe congestion, ckd, pulmonary edema, or already on oral furosemide. • if already on oral furosemide, iv starting dose should be at least equal to or higher than total daily oral dose. nice recommends iv diuretic therapy for acute heart failure, using either bolus or infusion strategy. monitor response panel answer: • urine output, • daily weight, • fluid balance, • dyspnea/orthopnea, • oxygen requirement, • crackles, • jvp, • edema, • bp, • creatinine/egfr, • sodium, • potassium, • magnesium. signs patient has decongested • can lie flatter, • reduced orthopnea/pnd, • reduced crackles, • reduced jvp, • edema improving, • weight loss, • negative fluid balance, • improved oxygenation, • improved hepatomegaly/ascites, • urine output improves. b. hypertensive acute pulmonary edema features: • severe dyspnea, • high bp, • pulmonary edema, • often preserved perfusion, • sympathetic surge. treatment 1. sit upright. 2. oxygen if hypoxic. 3. cpap/niv if severe. 4. iv furosemide if congested. 5. add nitrate if sbp allows. if sbp >110 mmhg: • sublingual gtn while preparing infusion, or • iv nitroglycerin infusion if available. avoid nitrates in: • hypotension, • severe aortic stenosis, • rv infarction, • recent sildenafil/tadalafil. c. cold-wet heart failure / cardiogenic shock this is dangerous. features: • hypotension or narrow pulse pressure, • cold extremities, • altered mentation, • oliguria, • delayed capillary refill, • high lactate/acidosis, • raised jvp/pulmonary edema/ascites. management 1. admit micu/hdu. 2. cardiac monitor. 3. oxygen/niv/intubation if needed. 4. avoid large blind fluids. 5. start vasopressor if hypotensive. 6. add inotrope if low cardiac output. 7. cautious diuresis after perfusion support if congested. 8. urgent echo and ecg. 9. treat cause: acs, arrhythmia, pe, infection, valve lesion. drugs noradrenaline infusion • start around 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min • titrate to map/perfusion, commonly map ≥65 mmhg. dobutamine infusion • start 2.5–5 mcg/kg/min • titrate according to bp, urine output, perfusion, lactate, rhythm. use noradrenaline for pressure and dobutamine for pump contractility. hold chronic hf drugs during shock hold/reassess: • beta-blocker, • acei/arb/arni, • spironolactone/eplerenone, • sglt2 inhibitor, • metformin, • nsaids. restart gradually once stable. d. cold-dry profile features: • cold peripheries, • low bp/low output, • no crackles, • low jvp, • no edema, • possible overdiuresis/dehydration. treatment give cautious fluid challenge: • 250 ml normal saline or ringer’s lactate • reassess bp, jvp, lungs, urine output, ivc/echo. if no response, stop fluids and use inotrope/vasopressor depending findings. 7. chronic hfref management — four pillars for hfref ef ≤40%, use four foundational classes if tolerated: 1. arni/acei/arb 2. evidence-based beta-blocker 3. mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist 4. sglt2 inhibitor aha/acc/hfsa identifies these as the main gdmt classes for hfref. pillar 1: arni / ace inhibitor / arb best international option sacubitril/valsartan is preferred over acei/arb in suitable symptomatic hfref patients. kcmc/tanzania practical alternatives if arni unavailable/costly, use acei or arb. enalapril • start 2.5–5 mg po od/bd • titrate upward as tolerated. losartan • start 25–50 mg po od • titrate to 100 mg od if tolerated. benefits • reduces mortality, • reduces hospitalization, • reduces remodeling, • reduces afterload. avoid/hold if • pregnancy, • bilateral renal artery stenosis, • angioedema history for acei, • severe hypotension, • aki, • k⁺ ≥5.5 mmol/l, • rapidly rising creatinine. monitoring check creatinine and potassium after starting or increasing dose. pillar 2: evidence-based beta-blocker start only when stable and euvolemic. options: carvedilol • start 3.125 mg po bd • titrate slowly. bisoprolol • start 1.25 mg po od • titrate slowly. metoprolol succinate • start 12.5–25 mg po od, if available. benefits • reduces mortality, • reduces sudden cardiac death, • reduces remodeling, • improves ef over time, • controls sympathetic overactivity. do not start/up-titrate if • acute pulmonary edema, • cardiogenic shock, • severe bradycardia, • heart block, • severe hypotension, • active bronchospasm. exam point if asked: “will you give beta blocker in adhf?” answer: “if patient is in shock, severe hypotension, bradycardia or acute pulmonary edema, i will hold or avoid starting beta-blocker. if already taking it and decompensation is mild with stable bp and no shock, i may continue cautiously. i start or uptitrate only after euvolemic and stable.” pillar 3: mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist spironolactone • start 12.5–25 mg po od • titrate if tolerated. alternative: • eplerenone if gynecomastia or intolerance and available. mechanism blocks aldosterone receptor → reduces sodium/water retention, potassium wasting, myocardial fibrosis and remodeling. benefits • reduces mortality, • reduces hf hospitalization, • helps resistant congestion. side effects • hyperkalemia, • worsening renal function, • gynecomastia, • breast tenderness, • menstrual irregularities. avoid/hold if • k⁺ ≥5.0–5.5 mmol/l, • severe renal impairment, • aki, • hypotension/shock. pillar 4: sglt2 inhibitor options: dapagliflozin 10 mg po od or empagliflozin 10 mg po od benefits • reduces hf hospitalization, • improves hf outcomes, • renal protection, • works even without diabetes in hfref. esc 2023 focused update strengthened sglt2 inhibitor use in hfmref and hfpef to reduce hf hospitalization and cardiovascular death. hold if • aki, • shock, • dehydration, • fasting/perioperative state, • dka/suspected dka, • severe acute illness. 8. diuretics in chronic hf diuretics relieve congestion but are not the main mortality-reducing therapy. furosemide practical dose: • 20–40 mg po od for mild congestion. • 40–80 mg po/iv or higher if severe/ckd. adjust to maintain euvolemia. monitor • weight, • urine output, • bp, • creatinine, • sodium, • potassium, • magnesium, • symptoms. diuretic resistance think of: • ckd, • high salt intake, • nsaid use, • poor gut absorption, • low renal perfusion, • venous congestion, • low albumin. management: • increase loop dose, • switch to iv, • consider infusion, • add thiazide-type diuretic if available, • consider dialysis/ultrafiltration if refractory overload. loop diuretics remain first-line for decongestion in congestive hf. 9. management of hfmref and hfpef hfmref ef 41–49% treat similarly to hfref when ef is near 40, especially if previous reduced ef. use: • diuretics for congestion, • sglt2 inhibitor, • acei/arb/arni in selected patients, • beta-blocker if ischemic disease, af, previous hfref, • mra in selected patients. hfpef ef ≥50% focus on: 1. diuretics for congestion. 2. bp control. 3. treat af. 4. treat ischemia. 5. treat obesity, dm, ckd, osa. 6. sglt2 inhibitor if eligible. 7. manage pulmonary hypertension/valvular disease if present. hfpef is not “normal heart failure.” the ef is preserved, but filling pressure is high. 10. management of right-sided hf / cor pulmonale common causes: • copd, • pulmonary hypertension, • ild, • chronic pulmonary tb, • pe, • left-sided hf, • tr. management: • treat underlying lung disease, • oxygen if hypoxic, • diuretics for systemic congestion, • avoid overdiuresis, • manage pulmonary hypertension cause, • anticoagulate if pe/dvt, • manage copd with bronchodilators, smoking cessation, ltot if indicated. signs: • raised jvp, • hepatomegaly, • ascites, • peripheral edema, • loud p2, • tr murmur. 11. af management in hf if unstable with hypotension, shock, pulmonary edema, chest pain: • synchronized dc cardioversion. if stable: • rate control, • anticoagulation based on cha₂ds₂-vasc, • treat trigger, • consider rhythm control if recent onset/symptomatic/hf worsening. drugs: • beta-blocker if stable hfref, • digoxin useful in hfref with low bp, • amiodarone if rhythm control needed or severe lv dysfunction. avoid: • verapamil/diltiazem in hfref due to negative inotropy. 12. anticoagulation in hf do not anticoagulate all hf patients automatically. indications: • af/flutter with stroke risk, • lv thrombus, • dvt/pe, • mechanical valve, • severe mitral stenosis with af. 13. non-pharmacological management lifestyle • salt restriction, • fluid restriction if hyponatremia or recurrent congestion, • daily weight, • stop smoking, • stop alcohol, • avoid nsaids, • exercise/cardiac rehab after stabilization, • vaccination where available, • adherence counseling. patient counseling in kiswahili “punguza chumvi kwenye chakula, epuka dawa za maumivu kama ibuprofen/diclofenac bila ushauri, tumia dawa zako kila siku, pima uzito mara kwa mara, rudi hospitali ukiona miguu inavimba zaidi, pumzi inaongezeka, unashindwa kulala chali, au uzito unaongezeka haraka.” 14. device therapy and referral consider cardiology referral for: icd for selected hfref patients with ef ≤35% despite optimized therapy and good expected survival. crt if: • ef low, • wide qrs, • especially lbbb, • persistent symptoms despite gdmt. valve intervention if severe mr, as, ar, ms, tr contributing to hf. coronary evaluation/revascularization if ischemic cardiomyopathy suspected. advanced hf referral refer if: • recurrent admissions, • ef \u003c25–30%, • inotrope need, • refractory congestion, • cardiorenal syndrome, • low bp limiting gdmt, • recurrent arrhythmias, • cachexia, • nyha iii–iv despite treatment. 15. management of complications a. cardiorenal syndrome mechanisms: • low cardiac output, • renal venous congestion, • raas activation, • diuretics/poor intake. management: • assess wet/dry and warm/cold, • maintain perfusion, • decongest carefully, • avoid nephrotoxins, • hold acei/arb/mra/sglt2i temporarily if aki/hyperkalemia/shock, • dialysis if aeiou indications. b. hyponatremia usually dilutional due to adh activation. management: • fluid restriction if severe/recurrent, • treat congestion, • avoid rapid correction, • monitor sodium. c. hyperkalemia common with aki, acei/arb/mra. if ecg changes/severe: • calcium gluconate, • insulin-dextrose, • salbutamol, • bicarbonate if acidotic, • dialysis if refractory. d. pleural effusion/ascites usually transudative from congestion. management: • treat hf with diuretics, • tap if unilateral, febrile, very large, atypical, or not responding. 16. monitoring inpatient hf daily: • symptoms, • bp/hr/rr/spo₂, • jvp, • edema, • chest crackles, • weight, • input/output, • urine output, • creatinine/egfr, • sodium/potassium, • oxygen requirement, • ecg rhythm if unstable. 17. discharge criteria discharge when: • clinically stable, • no worsening dyspnea, • oxygen stable/off if possible, • euvolemic or near-euvolemic, • on oral diuretics, • renal function/electrolytes stable, • gdmt started or plan documented, • patient educated, • follow-up arranged. nice recommends discharge after acute hf when clinical condition is stable and a management plan is in place. 18. follow-up plan within 1–2 weeks if recently admitted or medication changed: • symptoms, • bp/hr, • weight, • edema/jvp, • creatinine, • potassium, • sodium, • adherence, • titrate gdmt. long term: • optimize four pillars, • repeat echo after 3–6 months of therapy if hfref, • manage comorbidities, • vaccination, • education. 19. tanzania/kcmc vs international guideline comparison kcmc/tanzania practical approach common practical management: • abcde, • oxygen if hypoxic, • iv furosemide for congestion, • nitrates if hypertensive pulmonary edema and available, • noradrenaline + dobutamine for cardiogenic shock, • enalapril/losartan, carvedilol/bisoprolol, spironolactone, dapagliflozin/empagliflozin when stable, • echo-based management, • treat triggers: infection, anemia, af, acs, pe, renal failure, • dialysis if refractory overload/aki complications. aha/acc/hfsa / esc approach international approach emphasizes: • early gdmt with four pillars in hfref, • arni preferred where possible, • sglt2 inhibitors across hfref and now strongly in hfmref/hfpef, • iv iron in selected iron-deficient hf patients, • icd/crt when indicated, • advanced hf referral, • mechanical circulatory support/transplant in selected stage d hf. the major difference is availability and cost of arni, device therapy, cardiac mri, coronary intervention, transplant/lvad, and specialized hf clinics. 20. practical prescription-style examples stable hfref outpatient example if bp, renal function and k⁺ allow: 1. enalapril 2.5 mg po bd or losartan 50 mg od 2. carvedilol 3.125 mg po bd when euvolemic 3. spironolactone 25 mg po od if k⁺ acceptable 4. dapagliflozin 10 mg po od 5. furosemide 40 mg po od if congested 6. atorvastatin if ascvd/diabetes/high risk 7. salt restriction, daily weight, follow-up labs. acute congested hf admission example 1. sit upright. 2. oxygen if hypoxic. 3. ecg, cxr, fbp, u&e/cr, k⁺/na⁺, troponin if indicated. 4. foley if severe. 5. furosemide 40–80 mg iv stat. 6. monitor urine output and bp. 7. treat precipitant. 8. start/restart gdmt once stable. cardiogenic shock example 1. micu/hdu. 2. abcde, oxygen/niv/intubation if needed. 3. ecg, urgent echo, lactate, renal/electrolytes. 4. noradrenaline infusion for map/perfusion. 5. dobutamine infusion if poor contractility. 6. avoid blind fluids. 7. cautious diuresis if congested after perfusion support. 8. hold beta-blocker/acei/mra/sglt2i temporarily. 9. treat acs/arrhythmia/pe/infection/valve lesion. 21. common exam questions and answers q1. how do you know patient has heart failure? “by symptoms and signs of congestion or low output, supported by objective evidence. i would use history, examination, cxr, ecg, bnp/nt-probnp if available, and echocardiography.” q2. what is the definitive investigation? “echocardiography is key because it shows ef, chamber size, valves, wall motion, rv function, pulmonary pressures, pericardium and thrombus. bnp/nt-probnp supports diagnosis but does not replace echo.” q3. what do you monitor after furosemide? “urine output, weight, fluid balance, bp, dyspnea, jvp, edema, crackles, oxygen requirement, creatinine, sodium, potassium and magnesium.” q4. does ef change management? “yes. hfref needs four-pillar mortality-reducing therapy. hfpef management focuses on decongestion, bp control, comorbidity management and sglt2 inhibitor if eligible.” q5. will you give beta-blocker in acute hf? “not if the patient has cardiogenic shock, severe hypotension, bradycardia or acute pulmonary edema. i start or uptitrate beta-blocker only once stable and euvolemic.” q6. how do you manage hf with af? “if unstable, synchronized cardioversion. if stable, rate control, anticoagulation according to stroke risk, treat triggers, and avoid verapamil/diltiazem in hfref.” ward-round summary “management of heart failure starts by classifying the patient by ef, nyha class, acc/aha stage, and congestion/perfusion profile. in acute decompensated hf, i start with abcde, oxygen only if hypoxic, niv/cpap if
