1\u003c/figcaption>\u003c/figure>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Finger Clubbing and Edema\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Examination + Causes + How to Report\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Finger Clubbing\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Definition\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Finger clubbing is bulbous enlargement of the distal phalanges due to increased soft tissue at\u003cbr>the nail bed, with loss of the normal angle between the nail plate and proximal nail fold.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Normal Lovibond angle is about 160°.  In clubbing, it becomes &gt;180°.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">How to examine for clubbing\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 1: Inspect the fingers\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Look from the front and side for:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  bulbous swelling of terminal phalanges,\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 2\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  increased nail curvature,   •  shiny stretched skin,   •  loss of normal nail angle.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 2: Lovibond angle\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Look at the angle between the nail plate and proximal nail fold.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Normal: around 160°   •  Clubbing: &gt;180°\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 3: Schamroth window test\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ask patient to place the dorsal surfaces of corresponding fingers together, nail-to-nail.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Normally, there is a small diamond-shaped window between the nails.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In clubbing:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Schamroth window is lost.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 4: Fluctuation/sponginess of nail bed\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Gently press the nail bed.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In clubbing, the nail bed feels soft or spongy.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Grades of clubbing\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Grade\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Finding\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Grade 1\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Increased fluctuation/sponginess of nail bed\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Grade 2\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Loss of normal Lovibond angle\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Grade 3\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Increased nail curvature/parrot-beak nail\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Grade 4\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Drumstick appearance of distal phalanx\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Grade 5\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy: clubbing + painful periostitis of long bones\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Causes of finger clubbing\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A. Respiratory causes\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">These are the commonest in medical exams.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Bronchogenic carcinoma   2. Bronchiectasis   3. Lung abscess\u003c/h3>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 3\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">4. Empyema\u003cbr>5. Interstitial lung disease\u003cbr>6. Cystic fibrosis\u003cbr>7. Pulmonary tuberculosis, especially chronic/fibrocavitary disease\u003cbr>8. Mesothelioma\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Important exam point:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">COPD alone does not usually cause clubbing.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If a COPD patient has clubbing, think of:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  lung cancer,   •  bronchiectasis,   •  ILD,   •  chronic suppurative lung disease.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">B. Cardiac causes\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Cyanotic congenital heart disease   2. Infective endocarditis   3. Atrial myxoma\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">C. Gastrointestinal and liver causes\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Inflammatory bowel disease\u003cbr>2. Liver cirrhosis\u003cbr>3. Primary biliary cholangitis\u003cbr>4. Malabsorption / coeliac disease\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">D. Endocrine cause\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Thyroid acropachy in Graves’ disease\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">How to report clubbing in examination\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Say:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“There is bilateral grade ___ finger clubbing, evidenced by loss of Schamroth window and  increased Lovibond angle.”\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 4\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Example:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“There is bilateral grade 3 finger clubbing with loss of Schamroth window and increased nail\u003cbr>curvature, suggesting chronic pulmonary disease such as bronchiectasis, ILD, lung malignancy,\u003cbr>or chronic pulmonary TB.”\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Edema\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Definition\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Edema is abnormal accumulation of fluid in the interstitial tissue. Clinically, it appears as\u003cbr>swelling, commonly in the lower limbs, sacrum, face, abdomen, or generalized body.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Types of edema\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A. Pitting edema\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">When you press the swollen area, it leaves an indentation.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Causes:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>heart failure,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>renal disease,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>liver cirrhosis,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>hypoalbuminemia,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>venous insufficiency,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>DVT,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>drugs such as amlodipine.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">B. Non-pitting edema\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">No indentation remains after pressure.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Causes:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  lymphoedema,   •  myxedema,   •  chronic advanced edema with fibrosis.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">How to examine lower limb edema\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 1: Expose both legs\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Expose from feet to knees or thighs.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Inspect for:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 5\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>swelling,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>symmetry,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>skin color,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>ulcers,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>varicose veins,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>scars,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>tenderness,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>cellulitis,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>signs of DVT.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 2: Press for pitting\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Use your thumb and press firmly for 5 seconds over:\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. dorsum of foot,   2. medial malleolus,   3. shin/tibia,   4. sacrum if bedbound.\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Then release and look for a pit.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 3: Grade pitting edema\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Grade\u003cbr>Description\u003cbr>1+\u003cbr>Mild pit, disappears rapidly\u003cbr>2+\u003cbr>Moderate pit, disappears in 10–15 seconds\u003cbr>3+\u003cbr>Deep pit, lasts &gt;1 minute\u003cbr>4+\u003cbr>Very deep pit, gross swelling, lasts several minutes\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 4: State the level\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Say how far the edema extends:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>pedal edema,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>ankle edema,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>up to mid-shin,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>up to knees,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>up to thighs,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>sacral edema,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>generalized edema/anasarca.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 5: Check if unilateral or bilateral\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Bilateral edema suggests:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 6\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>heart failure,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>CKD/nephrotic syndrome,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>liver cirrhosis,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>hypoalbuminemia,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>drugs,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>chronic venous insufficiency.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Unilateral edema suggests:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  DVT,   •  cellulitis,   •  lymphoedema,   •  trauma,   •  venous obstruction.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Causes of bilateral pitting lower limb edema\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Heart failure\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mechanism:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Right-sided congestion → raised venous pressure → fluid leaks into tissues\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Clues:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>raised JVP,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>hepatomegaly,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>ascites,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>basal crackles,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>orthopnea/PND,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>displaced apex,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>S3 gallop.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. CKD / renal failure\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mechanism:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Salt and water retention → volume overload\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Clues:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  oliguria,   •  hypertension,   •  high creatinine/urea,   •  pulmonary edema,   •  anemia,\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 7\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  uremic symptoms.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">3. Nephrotic syndrome\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mechanism:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Heavy protein loss in urine → hypoalbuminemia → reduced oncotic pressure\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Clues:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>facial puffiness,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>frothy urine,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>massive edema,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>proteinuria 3+ or 4+,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>low albumin,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>hyperlipidemia.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">4. Liver cirrhosis\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mechanism:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Low albumin + portal hypertension + sodium/water retention\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Clues:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>ascites,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>jaundice,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>spider naevi,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>palmar erythema,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>splenomegaly,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>varices,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>low albumin,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>raised INR.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">5. Drugs\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Common drugs:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  amlodipine/nifedipine,   •  NSAIDs,   •  steroids,   •  thiazolidinediones such as pioglitazone.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">6. Venous insufficiency\u003c/h3>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Clues:\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 8\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  worse in evening,   •  varicose veins,   •  hyperpigmentation,   •  venous ulcers,   •  improves with leg elevation.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Causes of unilateral lower limb edema\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Important causes\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. Deep vein thrombosis\u003cbr>2. Cellulitis\u003cbr>3. Lymphoedema\u003cbr>4. Trauma\u003cbr>5. Ruptured Baker’s cyst\u003cbr>6. Venous obstruction/compression\u003cbr>7. Post-thrombotic syndrome\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">DVT clues\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>unilateral swelling,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>calf pain,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>warmth,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>tenderness,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pitting edema,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>calf circumference difference &gt;3 cm,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>superficial collateral veins.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">How to report edema\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Good reporting:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“There is bilateral pitting pedal edema extending up to the knees, grade 2, with no calf\u003cbr>tenderness or skin discoloration.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If heart failure:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“There is bilateral grade 2 pitting lower limb edema up to the mid-shin, supporting systemic\u003cbr>venous congestion from right-sided or congestive heart failure.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If unilateral:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“There is unilateral left lower limb pitting edema up to the calf with calf tenderness and\u003cbr>increased warmth, concerning for DVT.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Exam link: clubbing + edema\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 9\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If patient has clubbing and edema, think of diseases causing both pulmonary and systemic  involvement.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Important combinations:\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Clubbing + edema may\u003cbr>suggest\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Why\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Lung cancer\u003c/td>\u003ctd>clubbing + cachexia; edema may be DVT, hypoalbumin, SVC\u003cbr>obstruction\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Bronchiectasis\u003c/td>\u003ctd>clubbing + chronic infection; edema if cor pulmonale\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>ILD\u003c/td>\u003ctd>clubbing + pulmonary hypertension/right HF\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Chronic pulmonary TB\u003c/td>\u003ctd>clubbing + cor pulmonale or hypoalbuminemia\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Cyanotic heart disease\u003c/td>\u003ctd>clubbing + heart failure\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Infective endocarditis\u003c/td>\u003ctd>clubbing + heart failure/immune phenomena\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Liver cirrhosis\u003c/td>\u003ctd>clubbing + hypoalbuminemia/ascites/edema\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ward-round summary\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“Finger clubbing is examined by inspecting nail curvature, checking Lovibond angle, Schamroth\u003cbr>window and nail-bed fluctuation, then grading from grade 1 nail-bed sponginess to grade 5\u003cbr>hypertrophic osteoarthropathy. Important causes are bronchogenic carcinoma, bronchiectasis,\u003cbr>ILD, lung abscess, empyema, cyanotic heart disease, infective endocarditis and cirrhosis. Edema\u003cbr>should be described as pitting or non-pitting, unilateral or bilateral, graded from 1+ to 4+, and\u003cbr>the level stated. Bilateral pitting edema suggests heart failure, CKD, nephrotic syndrome,\u003cbr>cirrhosis, drugs or venous insufficiency; unilateral edema suggests DVT, cellulitis or\u003cbr>lymphoedema.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Splenomegaly and Hepatomegaly — Examination + Causes + How to Report\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">1. Splenomegaly\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Definition\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Splenomegaly means enlargement of the spleen beyond its normal size. Clinically, a palpable\u003cbr>spleen usually indicates enlargement because a normal adult spleen is usually not palpable.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 10\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In exams, do not just say “spleen palpable.” Describe it properly.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">How to examine for splenomegaly\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 1: Position and exposure\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Place the patient supine, expose from chest to groin, and stand on the patient’s right side.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ask the patient to bend knees slightly to relax abdominal muscles.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 2: Start superficial palpation from the right iliac fossa\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">This is important. Enlarged spleen grows from left hypochondrium toward the right iliac\u003cbr>fossa. Therefore, if you suspect a huge spleen, start far away from it.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Start at:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Right iliac fossa → move diagonally toward left hypochondrium.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ask the patient to take deep breaths in and out. The spleen moves downward during inspiration.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 3: Deep palpation\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">After superficial palpation, use deep palpation along the same direction: from right iliac fossa\u003cbr>toward left costal margin.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Feel for:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  lower border,   •  notch,   •  tenderness,   •  consistency,   •  surface,   •  movement with respiration.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Step 4: Percussion\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Percuss Traube’s space or percuss from the right iliac fossa toward left hypochondrium to assess  dullness.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 5: Bimanual palpation\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">If not felt easily, place your left hand behind the left lower ribs and lift the spleen anteriorly\u003cbr>while palpating with the right hand.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Features confirming splenomegaly\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 11\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A spleen has these clinical features:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. It arises from the left hypochondrium.\u003cbr>2. It enlarges inferomedially toward the right iliac fossa.\u003cbr>3. It has a notch on the medial border.\u003cbr>4. You cannot get above it.\u003cbr>5. It moves with respiration.\u003cbr>6. It is dull to percussion.\u003cbr>7. It is usually not ballotable.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">How to describe splenomegaly\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Report:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>site/location,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>size below left costal margin,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>tenderness,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>consistency,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>surface,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>edge,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>notch present/absent,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>movement with respiration,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>associated ascites/lymph nodes/hepatomegaly.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Example:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“There is splenomegaly, palpable 6 cm below the left costal margin along the splenic axis. It is\u003cbr>firm, non-tender, smooth-surfaced, with a palpable notch, dull to percussion, and moves with\u003cbr>respiration.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Grading splenomegaly\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Clinical grading\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Grade\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Description\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Mild\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Just palpable below left costal margin\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003ctd>\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Moderate\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Palpable halfway between left costal margin and umbilicus\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Massive\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Extends beyond umbilicus or toward right iliac fossa\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hackett’s grading — commonly used in malaria/endemic splenomegaly\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Grade\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Description\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>0\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Not palpable\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>1\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Palpable only on deep inspiration\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>2\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Palpable below costal margin but above halfway to umbilicus\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 12\u003c/div>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>3\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Enlarged to halfway between costal margin and umbilicus\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>4\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Enlarged below umbilicus but not to pelvis\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>5\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Extends to pelvis/right iliac fossa\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Causes of splenomegaly\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Use categories.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A. Congestive causes\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">These are common in portal hypertension.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Liver cirrhosis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Portal hypertension from schistosomiasis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Portal vein thrombosis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Right-sided heart failure/congestive hepatopathy\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Budd–Chiari syndrome\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mechanism:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Portal hypertension → splenic venous congestion → splenomegaly → hypersplenism →  thrombocytopenia/pancytopenia.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">B. Infective causes\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Malaria\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Infective endocarditis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Tuberculosis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>HIV\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>EBV infectious mononucleosis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Visceral leishmaniasis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Typhoid\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Brucellosis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Viral hepatitis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">C. Hematological causes\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Hemolytic anemia\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Sickle cell disease early childhood, though later autosplenectomy may occur\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Thalassemia\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Leukemia\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Lymphoma\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Myelofibrosis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Polycythemia vera\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Chronic myeloid leukemia\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 13\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Massive splenomegaly strongly suggests:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>chronic myeloid leukemia,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>myelofibrosis,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>visceral leishmaniasis,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>lymphoma,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Gaucher disease.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">D. Autoimmune/inflammatory causes\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  SLE   •  Rheumatoid arthritis/Felty syndrome   •  Sarcoidosis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">E. Storage/infiltrative causes\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Gaucher disease   •  Amyloidosis   •  Niemann–Pick disease\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Differential diagnosis of tender splenomegaly\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Tender spleen is high-yield because your friends were asked.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Causes include:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. Splenic infarction\u003cbr>2. Splenic abscess\u003cbr>3. Malaria\u003cbr>4. Infective endocarditis with splenic infarcts/abscess\u003cbr>5. Acute leukemia\u003cbr>6. Lymphoma\u003cbr>7. Trauma/subcapsular hematoma\u003cbr>8. EBV infectious mononucleosis\u003cbr>9. Portal vein thrombosis or splenic vein thrombosis\u003cbr>10. Hemorrhagic fever/severe systemic infection\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Clinical clue:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Tender spleen + fever = think malaria, splenic abscess, endocarditis, EBV, leukemia,  hemorrhagic fever.\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Hypersplenism\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hypersplenism means enlarged spleen causing excessive sequestration/destruction of blood cells.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 14\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Features:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  splenomegaly,   •  anemia,   •  leukopenia,   •  thrombocytopenia,   •  bone marrow usually normal or hypercellular.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In portal hypertension, low platelets may be due to hypersplenism. That is why in UGIB/portal\u003cbr>HTN, FBP helps assess both Hb and platelets.\u003c/p>\u003ch3 class=\"note-text-block\">2. Hepatomegaly\u003c/h3>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Definition\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hepatomegaly means enlargement of the liver. Clinically, it is detected by palpating or\u003cbr>percussing a liver edge below the right costal margin or by increased liver span.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Important: A palpable liver is not always enlarged. It may be palpable in:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  thin patient,   •  hyperinflated lungs/COPD pushing liver down,   •  Riedel’s lobe.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">So always assess liver span.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">How to examine for hepatomegaly\u003c/p>\u003ch4 class=\"note-text-block\">Step 1: Position\u003c/h4>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Patient supine, head supported, abdomen exposed from chest to groin.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ask patient to relax and bend knees slightly.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 2: Start palpation from right iliac fossa\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Start low in the right iliac fossa and move upward toward the right costal margin in the  midclavicular line.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ask the patient to breathe deeply. The liver moves down during inspiration.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 3: Feel the liver edge\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Describe:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  distance below right costal margin,\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 15\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  tenderness,   •  consistency,   •  edge,   •  surface,   •  pulsatility,   •  movement with respiration.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Step 4: Percuss liver span\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Percuss in the right midclavicular line.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">1. Percuss from chest downward until resonance changes to dullness = upper border.\u003cbr>2. Percuss from abdomen upward until tympany changes to dullness = lower border.\u003cbr>3. Measure the distance between upper and lower borders.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Normal adult liver span is roughly:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">6–12 cm in the right midclavicular line, depending on body size.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">How to describe hepatomegaly\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Report:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>size below costal margin,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>liver span,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>tenderness,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>consistency,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>surface,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>edge,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>pulsatility,\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>associated signs: jaundice, ascites, splenomegaly, stigmata of CLD.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Example:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“The liver is enlarged, palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin in the midclavicular line,\u003cbr>smooth-surfaced, firm, non-tender, with a regular edge, moving with respiration. Liver span is 14\u003cbr>cm.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Liver edge interpretation\u003c/p>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Finding\u003c/td>\u003ctd>Suggests\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Soft tender liver\u003c/td>\u003ctd>acute hepatitis, congestive hepatopathy\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Firm smooth liver\u003c/td>\u003ctd>fatty liver, early cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Hard irregular/nodular\u003cbr>liver\u003c/td>\u003ctd>cirrhosis, malignancy\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Pulsatile liver\u003c/td>\u003ctd>tricuspid regurgitation\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 16\u003c/div>\u003cdiv class=\"table-scroll\">\u003ctable class=\"clinical-table\">\u003ctr>\u003ctd>Very tender enlarged liver\u003c/td>\u003ctd>acute hepatitis, hepatic abscess, congestive hepatopathy, Budd–\u003cbr>Chiari\u003c/td>\u003c/tr>\u003c/table>\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Causes of hepatomegaly\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">A. Infective/inflammatory\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Viral hepatitis: A, B, C, E\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Malaria\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Liver abscess: amoebic or pyogenic\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Leptospirosis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Infectious mononucleosis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>HIV-related liver disease\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">B. Congestive/vascular\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•\u003cbr>Right-sided heart failure\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Tricuspid regurgitation\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Constrictive pericarditis\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Budd–Chiari syndrome\u003cbr>•\u003cbr>Hepatic vein congestion\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Mechanism in heart failure:\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Raised right atrial pressure → hepatic venous congestion → tender hepatomegaly →  congestive hepatopathy → ascites.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">In tricuspid regurgitation, the liver may be pulsatile.\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">C. Metabolic/fatty liver\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  MASLD/NAFLD   •  Alcohol-associated liver disease   •  Diabetes mellitus   •  Obesity   •  Hyperlipidemia\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">D. Malignancy/infiltrativ\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Hepatocellular carcinoma   •  Liver metastases   •  Lymphoma/leukemia infiltration   •  Amyloidosis\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Usually hard, irregular, nodular, sometimes tender.\u003c/p>\u003c/section>\u003csection class=\"page-group\">\u003cdiv class=\"page-label\">PAGE 17\u003c/div>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">E. Storage/genetic\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Hemochromatosis   •  Wilson disease   •  Glycogen storage disease   •  Gaucher disease\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">F. Biliary/cholestatic\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">•  Primary biliary cholangitis   •  Primary sclerosing cholangitis   •  Biliary obstruction   •  Cholangiocarcinoma\u003c/p>\u003ch4 It is firm, smooth, non-tender, with a palpable notch, dull to percussion,\u003cbr>and moves with respiration. I cannot get above it.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Hepatomegaly report\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“The liver is palpable 5 cm below the right costal margin in the midclavicular line. It is firm,\u003cbr>smooth, non-tender, with a regular edge and moves with respiration. In this patient with\u003cbr>hematemesis and ascites, this supports portal hypertension, likely from chronic liver disease or\u003cbr>schistosomiasis.”\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">Ward-round summary\u003c/p>\u003cp class=\"note-text-block\">“Splenomegaly is examined by starting palpation from the right iliac fossa and moving\u003cbr>diagonally toward the left hypochondrium. A spleen enlarges inferomedially, has a notch, is dull\u003cbr>to percussion, moves with respiration and you cannot get above it. Causes include portal\u003cbr>hypertension, malaria, TB, HIV, endocarditis, leukemia, lymphoma and hemolytic anemia.\u003cbr>Hepatomegaly is examined by palpating from the right iliac fossa toward the right costal margin\u003cbr>and measuring liver span by percussion in the midclavicular line. Describe size, tenderness,\u003cbr>consistency, surface, edge and pulsatility. Causes include viral hepatitis, fatty liver, alcohol, right\u003cbr>heart failure, hepatic congestion, liver abscess, malignancy and infiltrative disease.”\u003c/p>\u003c/section>"}],"words":2736,"searchtext":" finger clubbing and edema examination + causes + how to report 1. finger clubbing definition finger clubbing is bulbous enlargement of the distal phalanges due to increased soft tissue at the nail bed, with loss of the normal angle between the nail plate and proximal nail fold. normal lovibond angle is about 160°. in clubbing, it becomes >180°. how to examine for clubbing step 1: inspect the fingers look from the front and side for: • bulbous swelling of terminal phalanges, • increased nail curvature, • shiny stretched skin, • loss of normal nail angle. step 2: lovibond angle look at the angle between the nail plate and proximal nail fold. • normal: around 160° • clubbing: >180° step 3: schamroth window test ask patient to place the dorsal surfaces of corresponding fingers together, nail-to-nail. normally, there is a small diamond-shaped window between the nails. in clubbing: schamroth window is lost. step 4: fluctuation/sponginess of nail bed gently press the nail bed. in clubbing, the nail bed feels soft or spongy. grades of clubbing grade finding grade 1 increased fluctuation/sponginess of nail bed grade 2 loss of normal lovibond angle grade 3 increased nail curvature/parrot-beak nail grade 4 drumstick appearance of distal phalanx grade 5 hypertrophic osteoarthropathy: clubbing + painful periostitis of long bones causes of finger clubbing a. respiratory causes these are the commonest in medical exams. 1. bronchogenic carcinoma 2. bronchiectasis 3. lung abscess 4. empyema 5. interstitial lung disease 6. cystic fibrosis 7. pulmonary tuberculosis, especially chronic/fibrocavitary disease 8. mesothelioma important exam point: copd alone does not usually cause clubbing. if a copd patient has clubbing, think of: • lung cancer, • bronchiectasis, • ild, • chronic suppurative lung disease. b. cardiac causes 1. cyanotic congenital heart disease 2. infective endocarditis 3. atrial myxoma c. gastrointestinal and liver causes 1. inflammatory bowel disease 2. liver cirrhosis 3. primary biliary cholangitis 4. malabsorption / coeliac disease d. endocrine cause 1. thyroid acropachy in graves’ disease how to report clubbing in examination say: “there is bilateral grade ___ finger clubbing, evidenced by loss of schamroth window and increased lovibond angle.” example: “there is bilateral grade 3 finger clubbing with loss of schamroth window and increased nail curvature, suggesting chronic pulmonary disease such as bronchiectasis, ild, lung malignancy, or chronic pulmonary tb.” 2. edema definition edema is abnormal accumulation of fluid in the interstitial tissue. clinically, it appears as swelling, commonly in the lower limbs, sacrum, face, abdomen, or generalized body. types of edema a. pitting edema when you press the swollen area, it leaves an indentation. causes: • heart failure, • renal disease, • liver cirrhosis, • hypoalbuminemia, • venous insufficiency, • dvt, • drugs such as amlodipine. b. non-pitting edema no indentation remains after pressure. causes: • lymphoedema, • myxedema, • chronic advanced edema with fibrosis. how to examine lower limb edema step 1: expose both legs expose from feet to knees or thighs. inspect for: • swelling, • symmetry, • skin color, • ulcers, • varicose veins, • scars, • tenderness, • cellulitis, • signs of dvt. step 2: press for pitting use your thumb and press firmly for 5 seconds over: 1. dorsum of foot, 2. medial malleolus, 3. shin/tibia, 4. sacrum if bedbound. then release and look for a pit. step 3: grade pitting edema grade description 1+ mild pit, disappears rapidly 2+ moderate pit, disappears in 10–15 seconds 3+ deep pit, lasts >1 minute 4+ very deep pit, gross swelling, lasts several minutes step 4: state the level say how far the edema extends: • pedal edema, • ankle edema, • up to mid-shin, • up to knees, • up to thighs, • sacral edema, • generalized edema/anasarca. step 5: check if unilateral or bilateral bilateral edema suggests: • heart failure, • ckd/nephrotic syndrome, • liver cirrhosis, • hypoalbuminemia, • drugs, • chronic venous insufficiency. unilateral edema suggests: • dvt, • cellulitis, • lymphoedema, • trauma, • venous obstruction. causes of bilateral pitting lower limb edema 1. heart failure mechanism: right-sided congestion → raised venous pressure → fluid leaks into tissues clues: • raised jvp, • hepatomegaly, • ascites, • basal crackles, • orthopnea/pnd, • displaced apex, • s3 gallop. 2. ckd / renal failure mechanism: salt and water retention → volume overload clues: • oliguria, • hypertension, • high creatinine/urea, • pulmonary edema, • anemia, • uremic symptoms. 3. nephrotic syndrome mechanism: heavy protein loss in urine → hypoalbuminemia → reduced oncotic pressure clues: • facial puffiness, • frothy urine, • massive edema, • proteinuria 3+ or 4+, • low albumin, • hyperlipidemia. 4. liver cirrhosis mechanism: low albumin + portal hypertension + sodium/water retention clues: • ascites, • jaundice, • spider naevi, • palmar erythema, • splenomegaly, • varices, • low albumin, • raised inr. 5. drugs common drugs: • amlodipine/nifedipine, • nsaids, • steroids, • thiazolidinediones such as pioglitazone. 6. venous insufficiency clues: • worse in evening, • varicose veins, • hyperpigmentation, • venous ulcers, • improves with leg elevation. causes of unilateral lower limb edema important causes 1. deep vein thrombosis 2. cellulitis 3. lymphoedema 4. trauma 5. ruptured baker’s cyst 6. venous obstruction/compression 7. post-thrombotic syndrome dvt clues • unilateral swelling, • calf pain, • warmth, • tenderness, • pitting edema, • calf circumference difference >3 cm, • superficial collateral veins. how to report edema good reporting: “there is bilateral pitting pedal edema extending up to the knees, grade 2, with no calf tenderness or skin discoloration.” if heart failure: “there is bilateral grade 2 pitting lower limb edema up to the mid-shin, supporting systemic venous congestion from right-sided or congestive heart failure.” if unilateral: “there is unilateral left lower limb pitting edema up to the calf with calf tenderness and increased warmth, concerning for dvt.” exam link: clubbing + edema if patient has clubbing and edema, think of diseases causing both pulmonary and systemic involvement. important combinations: clubbing + edema may why suggest lung cancer clubbing + cachexia; edema may be dvt, hypoalbumin, svc obstruction bronchiectasis clubbing + chronic infection; edema if cor pulmonale ild clubbing + pulmonary hypertension/right hf chronic pulmonary tb clubbing + cor pulmonale or hypoalbuminemia cyanotic heart disease clubbing + heart failure infective endocarditis clubbing + heart failure/immune phenomena liver cirrhosis clubbing + hypoalbuminemia/ascites/edema ward-round summary “finger clubbing is examined by inspecting nail curvature, checking lovibond angle, schamroth window and nail-bed fluctuation, then grading from grade 1 nail-bed sponginess to grade 5 hypertrophic osteoarthropathy. important causes are bronchogenic carcinoma, bronchiectasis, ild, lung abscess, empyema, cyanotic heart disease, infective endocarditis and cirrhosis. edema should be described as pitting or non-pitting, unilateral or bilateral, graded from 1+ to 4+, and the level stated. bilateral pitting edema suggests heart failure, ckd, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, drugs or venous insufficiency; unilateral edema suggests dvt, cellulitis or lymphoedema.” splenomegaly and hepatomegaly — examination + causes + how to report 1. splenomegaly definition splenomegaly means enlargement of the spleen beyond its normal size. clinically, a palpable spleen usually indicates enlargement because a normal adult spleen is usually not palpable. in exams, do not just say “spleen palpable.” describe it properly. how to examine for splenomegaly step 1: position and exposure place the patient supine, expose from chest to groin, and stand on the patient’s right side. ask the patient to bend knees slightly to relax abdominal muscles. step 2: start superficial palpation from the right iliac fossa this is important. enlarged spleen grows from left hypochondrium toward the right iliac fossa. therefore, if you suspect a huge spleen, start far away from it. start at: right iliac fossa → move diagonally toward left hypochondrium. ask the patient to take deep breaths in and out. the spleen moves downward during inspiration. step 3: deep palpation after superficial palpation, use deep palpation along the same direction: from right iliac fossa toward left costal margin. feel for: • lower border, • notch, • tenderness, • consistency, • surface, • movement with respiration. step 4: percussion percuss traube’s space or percuss from the right iliac fossa toward left hypochondrium to assess dullness. step 5: bimanual palpation if not felt easily, place your left hand behind the left lower ribs and lift the spleen anteriorly while palpating with the right hand. features confirming splenomegaly a spleen has these clinical features: 1. it arises from the left hypochondrium. 2. it enlarges inferomedially toward the right iliac fossa. 3. it has a notch on the medial border. 4. you cannot get above it. 5. it moves with respiration. 6. it is dull to percussion. 7. it is usually not ballotable. how to describe splenomegaly report: • site/location, • size below left costal margin, • tenderness, • consistency, • surface, • edge, • notch present/absent, • movement with respiration, • associated ascites/lymph nodes/hepatomegaly. example: “there is splenomegaly, palpable 6 cm below the left costal margin along the splenic axis. it is firm, non-tender, smooth-surfaced, with a palpable notch, dull to percussion, and moves with respiration.” grading splenomegaly clinical grading grade description mild just palpable below left costal margin moderate palpable halfway between left costal margin and umbilicus massive extends beyond umbilicus or toward right iliac fossa hackett’s grading — commonly used in malaria/endemic splenomegaly grade description 0 not palpable 1 palpable only on deep inspiration 2 palpable below costal margin but above halfway to umbilicus 3 enlarged to halfway between costal margin and umbilicus 4 enlarged below umbilicus but not to pelvis 5 extends to pelvis/right iliac fossa causes of splenomegaly use categories. a. congestive causes these are common in portal hypertension. • liver cirrhosis • portal hypertension from schistosomiasis • portal vein thrombosis • right-sided heart failure/congestive hepatopathy • budd–chiari syndrome mechanism: portal hypertension → splenic venous congestion → splenomegaly → hypersplenism → thrombocytopenia/pancytopenia. b. infective causes • malaria • infective endocarditis • tuberculosis • hiv • ebv infectious mononucleosis • visceral leishmaniasis • typhoid • brucellosis • viral hepatitis c. hematological causes • hemolytic anemia • sickle cell disease early childhood, though later autosplenectomy may occur • thalassemia • leukemia • lymphoma • myelofibrosis • polycythemia vera • chronic myeloid leukemia massive splenomegaly strongly suggests: • chronic myeloid leukemia, • myelofibrosis, • visceral leishmaniasis, • hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly, • lymphoma, • gaucher disease. d. autoimmune/inflammatory causes • sle • rheumatoid arthritis/felty syndrome • sarcoidosis e. storage/infiltrative causes • gaucher disease • amyloidosis • niemann–pick disease differential diagnosis of tender splenomegaly tender spleen is high-yield because your friends were asked. causes include: 1. splenic infarction 2. splenic abscess 3. malaria 4. infective endocarditis with splenic infarcts/abscess 5. acute leukemia 6. lymphoma 7. trauma/subcapsular hematoma 8. ebv infectious mononucleosis 9. portal vein thrombosis or splenic vein thrombosis 10. hemorrhagic fever/severe systemic infection clinical clue: tender spleen + fever = think malaria, splenic abscess, endocarditis, ebv, leukemia, hemorrhagic fever. hypersplenism hypersplenism means enlarged spleen causing excessive sequestration/destruction of blood cells. features: • splenomegaly, • anemia, • leukopenia, • thrombocytopenia, • bone marrow usually normal or hypercellular. in portal hypertension, low platelets may be due to hypersplenism. that is why in ugib/portal htn, fbp helps assess both hb and platelets. 2. hepatomegaly definition hepatomegaly means enlargement of the liver. clinically, it is detected by palpating or percussing a liver edge below the right costal margin or by increased liver span. important: a palpable liver is not always enlarged. it may be palpable in: • thin patient, • hyperinflated lungs/copd pushing liver down, • riedel’s lobe. so always assess liver span. how to examine for hepatomegaly step 1: position patient supine, head supported, abdomen exposed from chest to groin. ask patient to relax and bend knees slightly. step 2: start palpation from right iliac fossa start low in the right iliac fossa and move upward toward the right costal margin in the midclavicular line. ask the patient to breathe deeply. the liver moves down during inspiration. step 3: feel the liver edge describe: • distance below right costal margin, • tenderness, • consistency, • edge, • surface, • pulsatility, • movement with respiration. step 4: percuss liver span percuss in the right midclavicular line. 1. percuss from chest downward until resonance changes to dullness = upper border. 2. percuss from abdomen upward until tympany changes to dullness = lower border. 3. measure the distance between upper and lower borders. normal adult liver span is roughly: 6–12 cm in the right midclavicular line, depending on body size. how to describe hepatomegaly report: • size below costal margin, • liver span, • tenderness, • consistency, • surface, • edge, • pulsatility, • associated signs: jaundice, ascites, splenomegaly, stigmata of cld. example: “the liver is enlarged, palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin in the midclavicular line, smooth-surfaced, firm, non-tender, with a regular edge, moving with respiration. liver span is 14 cm.” liver edge interpretation finding suggests soft tender liver acute hepatitis, congestive hepatopathy firm smooth liver fatty liver, early cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis hard irregular/nodular cirrhosis, malignancy liver pulsatile liver tricuspid regurgitation very tender enlarged liver acute hepatitis, hepatic abscess, congestive hepatopathy, budd– chiari causes of hepatomegaly a. infective/inflammatory • viral hepatitis: a, b, c, e • malaria • liver abscess: amoebic or pyogenic • leptospirosis • infectious mononucleosis • hiv-related liver disease b. congestive/vascular • right-sided heart failure • tricuspid regurgitation • constrictive pericarditis • budd–chiari syndrome • hepatic vein congestion mechanism in heart failure: raised right atrial pressure → hepatic venous congestion → tender hepatomegaly → congestive hepatopathy → ascites. in tricuspid regurgitation, the liver may be pulsatile. c. metabolic/fatty liver • masld/nafld • alcohol-associated liver disease • diabetes mellitus • obesity • hyperlipidemia d. malignancy/infiltrativ • hepatocellular carcinoma • liver metastases • lymphoma/leukemia infiltration • amyloidosis usually hard, irregular, nodular, sometimes tender. e. storage/genetic • hemochromatosis • wilson disease • glycogen storage disease • gaucher disease f. biliary/cholestatic • primary biliary cholangitis • primary sclerosing cholangitis • biliary obstruction • cholangiocarcinoma hepatosplenomegaly when both liver and spleen are enlarged, think broadly. important causes category causes infective malaria, hiv, tb, ebv, visceral leishmaniasis, viral hepatitis portal hypertension cirrhosis, schistosomiasis, portal vein thrombosis hematological leukemia, lymphoma, hemolytic anemia, myelofibrosis congestive right hf, constrictive pericarditis infiltrative/storage gaucher, amyloid, sarcoidosis autoimmune sle, felty syndrome exam connection: portal hypertension in a patient with ugib and splenomegaly, think: portal hypertension → esophageal varices → hematemesis/melena. portal htn features: • splenomegaly, • ascites, • caput medusae, • thrombocytopenia, • variceal bleeding, • portal hypertensive gastropathy. in tanzania, important causes include: • schistosomiasis periportal fibrosis, • chronic hepatitis b/c cirrhosis, • alcohol-related cirrhosis, • portal vein thrombosis. splenomegaly vs left kidney mass feature spleen left kidney direction of enlargement inferomedial downward notch may be present absent can get above mass no usually yes movement with respiration yes less marked percussion dull resonant colon may lie anterior ballotable usually no often ballotable location left hypochondrium flank/loin hepatomegaly vs right kidney mass feature liver right kidney movement with respiration yes less marked upper border continuous with liver yes no dullness can get above mass no if liver yes if kidney ballotable no yes edge may be usually rounded sharp/rounded percussion dull colon resonance may be anterior practical report examples splenomegaly report “on abdominal examination, there is splenomegaly palpable 8 cm below the left costal margin along the splenic axis. it is firm, smooth, non-tender, with a palpable notch, dull to percussion, and moves with respiration. i cannot get above it.” hepatomegaly report “the liver is palpable 5 cm below the right costal margin in the midclavicular line. it is firm, smooth, non-tender, with a regular edge and moves with respiration. liver span is 15 cm.” hepatosplenomegaly report “there is hepatosplenomegaly with a firm smooth liver palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin and a firm spleen palpable 6 cm below the left costal margin. in this patient with hematemesis and ascites, this supports portal hypertension, likely from chronic liver disease or schistosomiasis.” ward-round summary “splenomegaly is examined by starting palpation from the right iliac fossa and moving diagonally toward the left hypochondrium. a spleen enlarges inferomedially, has a notch, is dull to percussion, moves with respiration and you cannot get above it. causes include portal hypertension, malaria, tb, hiv, endocarditis, leukemia, lymphoma and hemolytic anemia. hepatomegaly is examined by palpating from the right iliac fossa toward the right costal margin and measuring liver span by percussion in the midclavicular line. describe size, tenderness, consistency, surface, edge and pulsatility. causes include viral hepatitis, fatty liver, alcohol, right heart failure, hepatic congestion, liver abscess, malignancy and infiltrative disease.”"},{"id":"pdf-5","disease":"Hemorrhagic stroke","label":"Clinical management","origin":"Hemorrhagic Stroke Management
